subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would direct a question to the Minister of Justice. When he spoke on television last night at eleven o'clock and stated that he had no knowledge of the whereabouts of Mr. Banks, did he not at that time have the information that Mr. Murphy, a radio man connected with station CFRA, I believe, had had a radio discussion with Mr. Banks, and that Mr. Reguly of the Toronto Star just walked down by the dockside and was able to see Mr. Banks there along with his car bearing a Quebec licence? Would the minister be able to explain that rather incongruous position?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the right hon. gentleman knows, of course, one does not appear directly on television on the eleven o'clock news. These interviews are taped, and the interview in question was taped around 4.30 yesterday afternoon. I learned of this alleged interview with Banks at the time the interview was taped and I had no way, of course, of ascertaining to what extent the facts as alleged were accurate and especially no way
of ascertaining who tipped off the reporter. Whether or not it was Mr. Banks himself I do not know.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: I wonder whether the minister, having tried for so long to find the location of Mr. Banks, is now able to give us information with regard to whether the elusive Mr. Banks, the waltzing Matilda of Canadian politics, has been discovered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: I do not have precise information as to this yet, Mr. Speaker, and I repeat that I shall tell my right hon. friend whenever information is obtained.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the information the Minister of Justice gave the house yesterday in answer to the Leader of the Opposition, that the proceedings to which he referred could have been commenced five years ago, could the minister explain why those proceedings were not commenced during his tenure of office in the Department of Justice, which did not cease until 1960 after he had been there six years through two administrations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: Of course, Mr. Speaker, the information came to the Department of Justice in 1958, a period when a Liberal government, I am told, was not in office but rather a Conservative government; and the first positive statement came in February, 1962, at a time when a Liberal government was not in office.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. This does not answer the question-

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: Order. I do not wish to prevent anyone asking any reasonable and proper question at this time, but I suggest we are getting very close to starting a debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I wish to correct an inaccuracy. It was not February, 1962 as I have just stated, but February, 1959.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the point the minister raised yesterday is important and should be cleared up. Since the minister was serving as assistant deputy minister in the department in 1958, will he inform the house

speechtext: A supplementary question which I should like to direct to the Prime Minister. subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no such inquiry is necessary.
I think the facts are quite clear, and I do not think any useful purpose would be served at this time in establishing that kind of inquiry.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am still waiting for an answer from the Minister of Justice. Is he now in a position to say whether any inquiry was ever made of the immigration authorities in the United States as to Banks crossing the line with car attached? Second, can he say whether the S.I.U. office or Mr. Hall was ever communicated with to find out where Banks was?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I myself, of course, do not perform the actual investigations subsequent to demands for information. I never said in this house that a formal demand had been made to the immigration authorities of the United States. On the contrary, I said it was most unlikely that these would be the authorities who could supply us with information. What I did say in this 

respect was that the R.C.M.P. had asked the F.B.I. to supply us with information.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, did the minister notice the statement made by Paul Hall that he had never been asked where Banks was? Why did not the minister in the discharge of his responsibilities, if he was really trying to do something-

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS

subtopic: HAL BANKS-INQUIRY AS TO WHEREABOUTS

maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Minister of Justice, and ask him if his attention has been drawn to a statement made in the courts by Marcel Tardif to the effect he received guerrilla training in a secret camp last summer near Shawinigan? He says In his statement that this camp was used to give military training against "the enemy" and when asked by the judge as to who the enemy was he said "the federalists". I should like to ask the minister whether the R.C.M.P. have any knowledge of this alleged secret military camp or of any other secret military camps, and whether an investigation is being made by his department into the statement of Marcel Tardif.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: I have no knowledge personally to date of the facts as just stated. However, I shall take that question as notice and shall inquire.

maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Has the Minister of Justice or the R.C.M.P. any knowledge of one Frangois Schirm who, according to Marcel Tardif, is a one time French paratrooper and who was the commander in charge of this camp? Has the R.C.M.P. any knowledge of this man or his activities, or is any attempt being made to question him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: I think this is a question that ought to be put on the order paper.

maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: Surely when a man is named in the courts as being the commander of a secret military camp, that is something that ought not to be put on the order paper where it may lie for two or three months. Surely this is a matter which the Department of Justice and the R.C.M.P. ought to be looking into. When I ask the minister if his department or the R.C.M.P. know anything about this man, surely I ought not to be told to put the question on the order paper.

maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: The hon. member has stated the question twice now and the minister has said he will take notice of it and investigate. I think, although the question is extremely important and that is why it was allowed in the first place, the minister should have an opportunity to make a full and complete investigation.

maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the minister did not say he would look into the matter of Frangois Schirm, who was allegedly the commander of this secret military camp. He asked me to put the question on the order paper. I am suggesting that this is a matter of too great urgency to be put on the order paper. If the minister will undertake to look into the question and report to the house, I am satisfied. However, I am not satisfied to put the question on the order paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: QUEBEC-REPORTED SECRET CAMPS FOR GUERRILLA TRAINING
speechtext:
The reason I suggested that the question be put on the order paper was that I thought Frangois Schirm was one of the three persons arrested and presently detained in Montreal in connection with a murder in an arms dealer's store. I shall inquire and, of course, any of these allegations or facts stated in newspapers are automatically and immediately inquired into by the R.C.M.P. Once the result of the inquiry is brought to my attention I shall report to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE ON MINES, FORESTS AND WATERS
speechtext:
That the subject matter of the water levels of the great lakes system be referred to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters for their consideration and report.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should perhaps make a very short statement in respect of this motion.
A nation rich in resources has the duty to ensure that her posterity never find it necessary to accuse their forefathers of neglectfully wasting their heritage. The present crisis in the livelihood and interests of many of our people in the great lakes basin requires that measures be taken which will not only meet current needs but will ensure the wise use of this water resource.
With these thoughts in mind I propose to introduce a motion on this subject. Before doing so I should like to report briefly to the house on measures already being taken by the government, and others which are now proposed, in regard to water levels in the great lakes. These measures form part of a comprehensive approach to the long term objective of learning to live with a natural resource of the size of the great lakes, but they also deal with today's problem.
As regards the current situation, I would remind the house that the international joint commission already has certain important responsibilities. Within the limits of natural conditions and existing authority it is regulating levels and flows from two of the lakes so as to make the best use of available supplies of water.
In April of this year all the lakes were below the average level of the past ten years for that month and, indeed, lake Huron reached its lowest level of the past 100 years. At the outlets of lake Superior and lake Ontario there are dams by which levels can be controlled but there are not present physical means by which the levels of lakes Michigan, Huron and Erie can be similarly regulated.
The commission's present authority extends only to lake Superior and lake Ontario. The international joint commission on June 25, 1964 authorized its lake Superior board of control to release water above the so-called "rule curve requirements" as long as supplies to the lake continue to be favourable and the present large differential in relation to low water datum between the 20220-549
Great Lakes Water Levels two lakes exists. This measure cannot provide an immediate end to the low water in the lakes downstream, but it will have a beneficial effect. It should be remembered that the time required for a larger portion of the benefit of this additional water to reach Montreal harbour will be well over one year because of the storage capacities of the intervening lakes and their relatively restricted outlet capacities.
Lake Ontario levels have been regulated since 1958 at the Barnhart island dam in the St. Lawrence, in accordance with the order of the I.J.C. Under the approved plan of regulation, levels on lake Ontario are maintained within a range of four feet during the navigation season, as contrasted with a range in nature of 6.6 feet. This has the effect of preventing as low a level of water in dry years as would have been the case had the Barnhart island dam not been built. There is every expectation that lake Ontario levels will be maintained within the improved range again this year. The levels of Montreal harbour are dependent on flows from the Ottawa river as well as from lake Ontario, and the approved plan of regulation recognizes this fact. In anticipation of low water supplies this year, every effort was made by the international joint commission and its board of control, in co-operation with the water users, to store as much additional water as possible in lake Ontario. This was released later in the season to alleviate expected low water conditions at Montreal and the lower St. Lawrence, when the flow from the Ottawa river fell off.
While the international joint commission is doing everything it can under its present authority, there are some steps the government can take to alleviate the worst effects of the present low water levels in particular harbours. On June 4 my colleague the Minister of Public Works informed the house of the expanded dredging program to be undertaken by his department. This dredging will relieve the local situation in some hard pressed areas, but I do not wish to imply that dredging can meet the needs of the many foreshore interests which are currently harassed by low water conditions or which may at other times suffer from high lake levels.
Indeed, the improvement of the water levels themselves is a longer term problem to which solutions must be found. One approach is to study the possibility of extending the regulation regime to make the best use of all the
8676	HOUSE OF
Great Lakes Water Levels water supplies available from the great lakes basin. Until there is complete knowledge as to how the waters of the basin can be controlled and interests protected through both wet and dry periods, we should be concerned about any plan to introduce large supplies of imported waters. Experience with international regulation of levels on lake Ontario and lake Superior confirms the fact that substantial benefits can be achieved by the regulation of outflows.
As the Prime Minister told the house on May 22, the governments of Canada and the United States are proceeding with a special reference to the international joint commission on great lakes water levels. I expect that an early agreement will be reached to study the feasibility of extending the present regulatory system. This study will take some considerable time and immediate results are not to be expected.
The whole problem of water levels in the great lakes basin is exceedingly complex. As I mentioned earlier, it is welded to the greater human problem of how to live with a natural resource that is unique both in kind and in size. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that there are certain aspects in nature which we can bend to a certain extent, and there are some which we cannot bend. An understanding of causes and possible solutions involves the examination of extensive and complicated technical data. The facets of this complicated problem must become better understood by all those both within and outside this house who are concerned with the problem. A close examination of and a concentration of public attention upon the facts of the situation seem imperative at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to the motion introduced by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I do not know if his statement was brief in order to get the matter before the committee or if he felt that enough had been said in the house so that members are sufficiently aware of the critical situation that exists.
We on this side are well aware of the need that exists for policy and action in regard to the many problems with which the provinces and municipalities are faced. However, you cannot take action without some policy. We believe it has gone far enough. We believe at this particular stage of the game there could be some policy statement made to indicate that action will be forthcoming in the very near future. Indeed, some of the people living in the area of this great water system expected that action would have been taken before this time. The great loss that has been suffered by resort owners, and the great loss that has been sustained as a result of the lack of action and the lack of policy, are things which the people concerned can no longer tolerate.
We are aware of the conflict that exists. I do not say this to the minister today in an endeavour to suggest that this problem is new, because it certainly is not new. It is an old problem. It is a problem that has existed for a considerable period of time. We know of the extensive areas of authorities concerned within this government itself. For instance,

Great Lakes Water Levels there are a number of departments involved such as external affairs, transport, mines and technical surveys, agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and even health and welfare; and of course public works is involved to a substantial degree. Action by one of these departments is not sufficient to protect the interests Of those served by other departments.
! I was interested to note that the minister himself stated lake Huron had reached the lowest level experienced in 100 years. Surely this would indicate that some type of practical action is necessary at an early date. I could refer back to the address that was made by the hon. member for Simcoe East, who brought this problem forcefully to the attention of the government on September 18. We did this previously as well. I think of the representations that were made to the government by the hon.. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue away back on May 11 by way of a motion. He felt the matter was of such immediate importance that he placed a motion on the order paper, and it was discussed at that time.
If action is to be taken, such as the development of policy, and if it is such as to bring pressure to bear upon the government, if this is the minister's own view, then we will support him wholeheartedly. However, we do hot believe government policy or action can be formulated by any such house committee. This must be the responsibility of the government. It was for this reason I stated we expected some action to be taken before this time.
I could refer also to speeches made by other hon. members, and I shall do so as briefly as 'I can, Mr. Speaker. I could refer to the contradiction which we believe has existed this year, and perhaps even before, within the government itself. I am thinking of a newspaper article that comes to us in the Vancouver Times. This article is by Mr. Dillon O'Leary, the Times Ottawa correspondent, anh the headline is "Lbing Contradicts Davis; Keep Water for Ourselves". The sentiment expressed here by the minister, that of keeping water for our own development, is certainly one with which I can agree. We believe water is one Of the most important resources Canada has today. The minister has made this statement. However, confusion 'exists when the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister makes one statement in B.C. and the minister contradicts him. This 'statement may relate to British Columbia and I realize I am getting away from the great

lakes, Mr. Speaker, but it indicates the confusion that exists.
Then I should like to refer to this well known and well documented article in the Montreal Gazette of September 12 written by the parliamentary correspondent, Mr. Arthur Blakely. This is a full page article which I think is most comprehensive. It outlines the problems which exist. It points out very forcefully some of the difficulties, such as, for instance, the way we lose this resource today. It may be that the minister will agree with me because I am one of those who believe that employing the virtuous course of prayer may be very desirable in connection with a question of this sort. Other questions have arisen here this morning in connection with which the same virtuous course might be employed with better results.
In this particular case Mr. Blakely has gone to great lengths to explain what the problem is and to outline the confusion. We on this side have known for a long time the confusion that exists. Mr. Blakely, for instance, deals very forcefully with the way we waste water. The heading on this article, of course, is "Canada's Water Going Down the Drain"; this is in a derogatory sense and not in the ordinary sense. He points out there have been floods causing immense property damage which could have been better controlled and, in many cases, avoided altogether. He deals with the question of shipping and the depletion of previously low levels; the supply of fresh drinking water without which great cities cannot exist; the virtual destruction of once great commercial fisheries. He goes into all the areas of concern such as recreation, soil, soil erosion, and so on. I think the last point he makes is a very good one. He refers to the dangerous tendency to allow Canadian water resources to be diverted outside our borders on a first come first served basis before Canada's own future requirements have been studied, let alone assured.
This is the thing with which I feel we must concern ourselves. We hope, of course, that Canada's population will be much greater in the future than it is today. If we are not sufficiently cognizant of this particular problem to do something about it, then I think we are going to lose for all time part of the resources that we have.
I come back to the proposal made by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue. He referred to the great problem that exists with regard to these resources and men-

tioned the plan of Mr. Thomas Kierans, a Sudbury engineer, for the diversion of water to supply our various needs. I believe, however, that the answers to the many problems that exist lie within our own competence.
Mr. Blakely goes on to refer to a conflict over the great lakes, and in his article he says:
It is scarcely surprising. Under the rambling, ramshackle Canadian control system-if it can be described as a system-solutions whether of the short term, medium term or long term, almost defy application.
It is a story everywhere, and at all levels, of divided jurisdiction.
I regret the reason which necessitates the Minister of Transport being absent from the house, but some time ago I asked him if the government had any policy to bring this matter under the jurisdiction of one department or one area of control. I forget the exact words of his answer, but he explained that this could not be done because of diversification of interests. Here is the nub of the thing, Mr. Speaker; there has to be leadership. Not only do we require policy and action but we need active, positive leadership, and in my opinion we do not have this leadership.
In his article Mr. Blakely went on to explain that there is a lack of hydraulic engineering authority from which the minister can draw advice. Nevertheless I believe we have enough qualified men to give us a start, if we could only eliminate the professional jealousy that exists between departments. I will excuse any of these officials if they will just drop this pettiness so far as their departmental positions are concerned, pool their resource knowledge and do something.
I have no qualifications in this field, but I understand the problem starts in the waters of the St. Lawrence downstream from Montreal, and that any solution must begin at that particular point. I believe it is lake St. Peter, though I am not absolutely certain of that. However, the solution or remedy should be undertaken there first; then work can proceed back up through the great lakes system.
As has already been said in the house, we should see what people have done in European countries to conserve their resources; then we could take some similar type of action. However, first and foremost we have to have a separate water authority, and if necessary we must convince our neighbours to the south that they should have a separate
Great Lakes Water Levels authority too, instead of both of us having a proliferation of semi-authorities, semi-areas of control which have no function and meaning in the question before us today.
I know, as does the parliamentary secretary to the minister, that reports exist within departments, very technical, substantive reports, dealing with a solution of this problem, but somehow or other the jealousies that exist between departments cause these reports to be pigeonholed and buried somewhere as official government documents not available to the public. Slowly but surely some of them are being drawn out. Mr. Blakely referred to this in his article, although we had known about it previously, and I am very pleased he saw fit to make it public knowledge. In regard to one report he wrote:
It recommended the installation of a system of dikes in lake St. Peter which would compress the river flow in that area.
Obviously this is the beginning of the solution, but I understand that a much lesser sum of money could have been spent in solving it than has been spent to date, and the solution here would have been the answer for the port of Montreal.
When one is not a professional one can only deal with the expert information that is placed before one. Therefore I say it is not an impossible situation. Far from it; I am told that if we can control the problem at this point a magnetic study shows that the flow of water can be so diverted as to keep the St. Lawrence open for a much longer period of the year. I know this is not pleasing to eastern Canada, but the hydraulic engineers know what can be done on the basis of their own knowledge and the experience of European countries.
The minister cannot expect the committee to give him the kind of direction he requires. He must find these things out himself, and I am sure he knows them now. Today he showed a willingness to participate in the answering of questions, which was a wonderful thing. It does not happen too often when we are questioning the government benches; therefore I compliment him in that regard. He gave some of the answers our people wanted to hear.
The hon. member for Simcoe East gave a good outline of the things that have been tried, of the things that must be tried and of the policy that must be adopted in order to eliminate the low water levels. The minister says levels have been interfered with from the point of view of man-made de-

Great Lakes Water Levels
vices, and I maintain that the problem can be dealt with in a similar way.
Recently when I was in Scotland I was interested to learn how resources were conserved there. The hydroelectric company of Britain-I forget the exact name-has taken the flow of water from a lake in its northern division and used it to drive turbines that supply electricity. It has installed an automatic system whereby when the peak consumer period passes the turbines are phased out and two of them are reversed to act as pumps, raising water from a large basin dredged out at the base of the power plant. The water is pumped back upstairs and reused next day. In fact during the night time when consumption is at its lowest, six turbines are reversed to pump water back up to the lake, to be used a second or possibly a third time for the generation of electricity. This shows there is already a means of conservation in operation and this may be the answer to our problem at Kingston. If not, there are other means which can be used to halt the catastrophic waste of water.
Today the hon. member for Danforth raised the question of the Credit valley control system, without receiving a satisfactory answer. We pray that the minister will press the government to take action. We shall not plead with him to the point where we will get down on our knees, because I think there is a greater authority than the minister, but we do hope he will see fit to press the government into some action to achieve the solutions we believe are possible.
As has been stated by my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka, there have been conferences before. This is why we have not too much to say about the setting up of a committee. Surely at these earlier conferences there were people present with more experience on these questions than those who will take part in the committee now proposed, with the exception, of course, of the expert witnesses who will be called. It is, naturally, my hope that the committee will have a free hand in the calling of witnesses.
The minister has mentioned the meetings held in Michigan, Toronto and Montreal. One would have thought that as a result of these meetings some clear policy or course of action on the part of the government would have emerged. If the delay so far has been due to any watering down of the remedies put forward by the authorities, let us put an end to it now. Let us do

something constructive. We may not have the opportunity again. When the growth of our country reaches a certain stage it will be much too late to begin anything on lines which are possible today.
Mr. Speaker, we are concerned with the conservation of water in areas of this country other than the great lakes and its associated system. My reference to this aspect will be brief because I realize I might be out of order, though of course this subject comes well within the competence of the minister whose motion is now before us. As I have indicated already, it is doubtful whether we really need a committee to consider water levels in the great lakes, because sufficient information must surely be available to the government as a result of the various conferences which have been held.
However, since the government has no particular policy to put forward we intend to support the setting up of a committee in the hope that as a result of pressure on the government some policy of action will evolve. I believe that if its work is to be effective the committee must be able to bring in outside witnesses such as Professor Langford, in addition to witnesses from the United States; because I think the problem in the United States is closely related to our own. There must be an indication from the government that it fully understands the efforts of our two countries in this field must be correlated. The Minister of Transport said this was not possible. Perhaps the minister of northern affairs will say the same thing, but I do not think his parliamentary secretary would agree with him. We feel there must be one policy, one course of action, one authority.
I wish to refer to the experience we have had in British Columbia; the great potential we have in the north and the fact that we may lose the possibility of developing a most valuable natural resource situated in the Yukon Territory. This most valuable resource may well be lost if we do not act quickly. I refer in particular to what is known as the Rampart scheme on the Yukon river. Its potential is many times that of the St. Lawrence seaway in hydro power alone. It involves a great body of resource water available for us to develop as Canadians.
We know there are alternatives which are currently under discussion. One is known as the Tulsaquan project and the other is the Tayia project; I believe those

are the correct pronunciations. We believe that this subject, because of its importance to the Canadian economy both now and in the future, should also be placed before the committee for consideration. If one of the alternatives I have mentioned were adopted we would lose the entire potential of the great body of water whose development is proposed. Other schemes would afford us at least a possibility of maintaining something for ourselves. I might mention, perhaps, that the Yukon river flows through Yukon Territory for a distance of 2,200 miles. It is the seventh largest navigable river in the world, and is extremely rich in resources of all kinds.
I therefore move, seconded by my hon. friend from Yukon:
That after the word "system" in the first line of the said resolution be added the following words: "and the proposal for the construction of a dam at Rampart in the state of Alaska on the Yukon river."
I do so in order that these matters may be discussed at one and the same time.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to rise to give support on behalf of the New Democratic party to the resolution before the house which will enable a committee of the house to undertake a thorough study of a most serious and complex problem, namely the water levels of the great lakes.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in a debate of this kind it is almost impossible to overemphasize or even to state adequately the importance of this great inland waterway to the economies of both Canada and her neighbour to the south. The existence of this waterway gives both the United States and Canada an inland development advantage over practically every other nation in the world. It supports the industries of some of our major cities such as Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor, Sault Ste. Marie and the lakehead as well as the limited United States cities of Buffalo, Cleveland, Detroit, Chicago, Milwaukee, Duluth and a host of others.
Unfortunately the problem of the water levels has in some degree become a cause of friction between the Canadian government, the provinces involved and some of the neighbouring states. This is regrettable, but it does emphasize the importance to the economies of both countries. Mr. Kierans, who has proposed a rather imaginative and expensive solution to the problem, has stated in a release:
We go from crisis to crisis until we really land ourselves in a jackpot. By 1975 we'll have the biggest crisis of all. If they keep fighting among themselves they'll have a disaster on their hands.
This view of the importance of the problem and the immediate necessity for some 20220-5501
Great Lakes Water Levels action is reinforced by Professor Kenneth Hare of McGill University, who says:
I think the great lakes water shortage is more profound than even Kierans estimated.
So there seems no doubt that the committee we are setting up is undertaking the study of an extremely important problem facing the Canadian economy as a whole. When you look at the present situation-I think for the benefit of the committee some of this information should be placed on the record, although the committee will receive additional information-the picture is one which creates a feeling of dismay. One of our regrets is that the committee should be given this task in what are really the dying months of the session. It is most unfortunate that an opportunity could not have been found earlier in the year to place this committee in action so that it might have been dealing with this problem while the house was preoccupied all summer with the question of a distinctive Canadian flag.
The reports that are available, Mr. Speaker, show that lake Huron is three feet below normal, the lowest level since 1860, and that lake Michigan is just as bad. Lake Ontario is down two feet and lake Erie a similar amount. The St. Lawrence river is at its lowest level in 30 years between Kingston and Iroquois, and Montreal harbour itself is just thirsting for water. This constitutes a gigantic and monstrous problem facing the entire inland waterway system, and the results of this condition are a staggering economic loss to Canada running into the millions. The low water levels affect the lives and the pocketbooks of every citizen in central Canada as well as those on the prairies, because the movement of grain is also affected. As I have said, the losses run into untold millions.
For example, in the iron ore trade alone the loss is estimated at $13 million. A total of 6,920,000 tons could not be carried because of the low water levels, which represents the seasonal capacity of 15 ships. Resort operators in the lake Huron and Georgian bay areas face economic ruin because of low water levels, high docks and the serious cutback in the tourist trade. In the first four months of 1964 alone Ontario hydro lost one and a quarter billion kilowatts of power, and if this continues for the whole year it will amount to a loss equal to the entire consumption of the city of Toronto for a whole year.
Grain shipments have been affected. The ships cannot take full loads, and every

Great Lakes Water Levels Georgian bay port with grain elevators is losing money. The Midland elevators, for example, are down six million bushels in capacity. The Sault Ste. Marie locks can only be used by small lake freighters, again occasioning considerable economic loss.
To property owners the loss is just as staggering and personal. The St. Clair river is at the lowest level since 1934. Over the winter sewage pipes were exposed and frozen, sand beaches have reverted to rocky shores, boats and boathouses are landlocked by the hundreds. Harbours all along the system are practically useless for long periods of the year.
I put these views forward to emphasize the tremendous economic losses that we have sustained as a result of this problem. I am not being particularly critical of the minister. We all listened to his speech this morning, and I realize that he is seriously concerned *with the problem and most anxious that something should be done. The real tragedy, of course, is that nothing has been done over the past five or six years even though the problem has been very evident. I think this is a sad reflection on the apathy and indifference of previous administrations.
As far as the causes are concerned there is a variety of opinion. Low rainfall and not enough snow seem to be the major problem. Greater evaporation has taken place. Some people blame the deepening of the channel at Sarnia for pulling the plug on lake Huron. Other people have advanced theories with regard to the Chicago diversion. In any event, there is not sufficient agreement on the causes and Certainly far less agreement on the solutions.

There have been conferences between Ontario and the bordering states, and again useful information is available. Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment for lunch I had been discussing the complexity of the problem and some of the economic repercussions and damages that flow from the low levels of the great lakes. I had been emphasizing the extremely difficult and gargantuan task the committee faces. It seems almost as though the ultimate solution from a long run point of view may well involve sums of money that are far beyond the capacity of any province or any state, and may ultimately evoke some sort of international partnership between Canada, the United States and the various provinces and states bordering the great lakes. The more one examines it, the more it seems that any permanent, long run solution is going to be one involving considerable expense.
By way of conclusion I just wanted to state several propositions which, in our view, the committee should take into consideration. We hope the committee, above all else, will try to come up with some concept of the role of the federal government in this whole problem, and that it will try also to come up with some suggestions as to the nature of the over-all lake control system which will be necessary to control the flow of water throughout the Whole of the inland system, rather than go into the idea of importing water into the system at this stage. This may be a secondary consideration. Above all else, we hope the committee will have associated with it on some permanent basis people from the water resources division, people who will be responsible to and who will work for the committee rather than for any particular department of government. I do not really see how a committee of this sort is going to handle this type of problem if it behaves in the normal way that committees of the house usually conduct their affairs. Because of the complexity of the matter, we hope that

the committee will have available to it the resources to retain any technical or professional help which may be needed, and any sort of clerical staff it will require.
We would like to see the committee empowered to sit even though the house may be in recess. It is not likely we will have a recess this fall, but the work of the committee should be continued. We hope it would continue. We hope some method could be found for a committee of this type continuing to meet, even though the session itself ends. I know our rules do not provide for such a contingency, but it seems a waste of time to set up this committee approximately two months before the session is likely to conclude, then wait four or five months at the next session for our committees to be constituted and begin their work. It would seem to us the personnel of this committee should be able to sit constantly and keep abreast of the work it is doing. In short, we want to be sure that this committee has every possible facility to enable it to attack this complex task, not only financially but in terms of personnel and staff.
In order that this desire can be clarified, I should like to move a simple amendment with which I am sure the minister will be in agreement. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe):
That the motion be amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
"and the committee be empowered to engage tech, nical and clerical personnel as it may deem necessary".
I think that if this is done it will greatly facilitate the work of the committee. We realize the important and complex task which is ahead and we wish it well in its endeavours.

Mr. Speaker, one must admire the very ingenious argument raised by the parliamentary secretary, but the complete answer to his proposition is that while it is true in the final analysis it is for the committee itself to come to a decision as to whether or not it should engage technical and clerical personnel, yet it can only invoke that authority after it has been given to it by the house.
I think this is a very sensible step to take at this time, rather than have the committee decide later, if it so wishes, that it wants this power, and then have to come back to the house for it. This is not saying to the committee, "You must exercise this authority; you must engage technical and clerical personnel." By adopting this amendment we are clothing the committee with the widest possible powers, saying to its members, "If you see fit to exercise all or any of these powers, here is the authority to do so," thereby obviating the necessity for them to come back here for that authority.
This is something which has been done by at least four committees this year, including the public accounts committee, the joint com-


mittee on consumer credit and the fisheries committee, and money is appropriated for the use of these committees under the pertinent appropriations act. This is a sensible and useful amendment to adopt at this time, leaving it to the committee, during the course of their deliberations, to indicate whether they want to exercise this power or not. If they do not, then they do not have to come back to the house, and I submit with deference that the amendment is completely in order.

Water shortage will be one of our major problems in the next decade. The motion before us deals with the watersheds running into the great lakes. The importance of this matter is apparent to the people in eastern Canada, but it should be part and parcel of a national policy.
It should be included within the framework of the policy which the government intends to pursue. I believe that according to the report which was made on the Fraser river it is proposed to build a dam on the north fork of that river, or on the McGregor river, for flood control purposes. This is another part of the same problem. We should I think be looking forward to a time when we may wish to use water for the transportation of materials in pipe lines. Plans for transportation by this means are now being made in Edmonton in connection with shipments of iron ore from the Peace river area. All these matters must be related to the motion now before us.

I should like to take this opportunity to thank hon. members opposite for the important contributions they have made. I think their suggestions are extremely valuable. I should like in particular to acknowledge the contribution made by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) and for his friendly attitude in withdrawing the amendment he put forward in order to clarify the matter and enable the work of the committee to be concentrated upon the first consideration before it, namely the level of the great lakes.
The hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) pointed out that the committee could not establish policy, and of course that is so. This is primarily a committee before which purely technical matters will be dealt with, and we hope that out of its deliberations we can derive a reliable and sound policy for the future. I wish to remind the house that our consideration of all these questions of our natural resources, particularly our water resources, dates back to the resources for tomorrow conference of 1961. I have paid tribute to that conference in the past and I express once again the hope that the magnificent assemblage of data which resulted from that conference could be made required reading for all Canadians. We face this difficulty, that these resources, including the waters which flow or tumble within the separate provinces, are a provincial resource and our provinces are naturally jealous of their rights. But to the extent that presenting the picture in total to the public will lead the public to recognize that it is within the power of a province to do something which will cause inestimable damage to a neighbouring province, we hope we shall be in the position soon when people everywhere will realize that, particularly with regard to waters which flow across provincial boundaries, there is such a thing as a national resource in Canada in which all Canadians can share.
I do want to claim that we have done, to date, as much as we can do. We have been in touch with the provinces concerned with regard to the possibility of diverting water supplies, or of possible diversions to areas where they are required. We are expanding enormously the amount of money to be spent on making the necessary studies of a national


water policy. I want to remind hon. members that time has been on our side in respect to water development in this country. I believe that even those who in 1955 supported the agreement made in the province of British Columbia at that time between the provincial government and the Kaiser people would admit, today, that they were in error. It was suggested then that the provincial government should permit the building of dams on the Columbia river in return for an income of $1 million a year. By waiting, as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has pointed out, and by realizing the tremendous importance of water in every sphere of activity, we have been able to conclude an agreement with our neighbour the United States under which by 1972 more than $500 million will be returned, in effect, for the use of that particular river.
I hope that out of the inquiry to be made by this committee, using the best technical people it is possible to obtain, there will come a conviction on the part of all Canadians of just how important these water resources are.

Mr. Chairman, before the estimates of this branch carry I want to make a few remarks to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, since I am aware he does not intend to make a further statement at this point. The older Indian people in the part of the country in which I live often say that many years ago, before the white man came to Canada in any numbers, the Indian had all the land and the white man had the Bible. These days it is the white man that has all the land and the Indian has the Bible.
I tell this by way of prefacing my remarks on the Indian claims commission and the legislation respecting it, which was supposed to have been introduced and processed by parliament. This one aspect of Indian affairs is deserving of most of the complaints by members on this side of the chamber, because the history of it is a pretty sorry mess in terms of the inability of the department to meet a most pressing need and a most pressing commitment. Because nothing has been done it is my opinion things would be better had it never been mentioned in the house and mentioned to the Indian people.
The basic obstacle separating the Indian and non-Indian people of Canada is a lack of trust on the part of the Indians in the dealings they have had with successive Canadian governments. There are countless examples in our history where the rights of Indian people were abrogated, curtailed, or taken away entirely. There are countless examples of treaties signed with the Indian people by governments that had no intention of living
8696	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration up to either the spirit or the letter of those treaties.
I can give the committee a good example from my own area in northern Canada, and which I am sure could be duplicated by many members. I have here a copy of treaty No. 11, signed on July 17, 1922 by the government of the day with the Indian people of the north. One of the statements by the commissioner in the opening part of it, talking about the difficulties they had getting Indian people to sign peace treaties, reads as follows:
The Indians seemed afraid, for one thing, that their liberty to hunt, trap and fish would be taken away or curtailed but were assured by me that this would not be the case.
That treaty was signed in 1922; yet in 1917, some five years earlier, the government of Canada had signed an international agreement with the governments of the United States and Mexico, in terms of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, which specifically limited the right of the Indian people to kill certain kinds of migratory birds at certain times of the year. Thus we had a treaty being negotiated and signed by the Indian people, presumably in good faith, yet five years earlier the same government had signed away the Indians' rights in entering into an agreement with the governments of the United States and Mexico.
We do not have to go back to 1922 to find more examples of this. The first day I entered this chamber, on May 31, 1963, a question was asked by the hon. member for Skeena, who has been no slouch when it comes to standing up for the rights of Indians-and in saying that I do not indicate he is a slouch in anything else either-and his question drew the attention of the Prime Minister to a decision handed down by Chief Justice McRuer in the Ontario supreme court, ruling that the Indians' right to hunt, trap and fish must be respected.
The hon. member asked the Prime Minister to see to it that the Ontario supreme court decision be communicated to all federal officers and agencies throughout the country, and to the provincial governments, to make sure in future the rights of these Indian people would not be infringed. In that part of his answer which was not facetious the Prime Minister said, as recorded at page 502 of Hansard for that date, "Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to do that..." Then he went on to make a jest, but those were the key words. In actual fact he did not, and many members have been besieged by other cases involving Indian people who have continued to be persecuted in the courts.
[Mr. Rheaume.l

Law officers and various crown agencies continue to harass the Indian people when they break game and fish laws which the chief justice of Ontario categorically ruled do not apply to the Indian people. It is little wonder then that the Indian says the white man speaks with a forked tongue, because our pattern of dealing with the Indians over the years has been one of promises and trusts broken, and outright betrayals.
There are ways of building trust with a group of people who may for the time being be socially and technologically under developed. The minister would do well to look at some of the things which occurred during the administration of the previous government. You build trust in people when you give them the right to vote, and for the first time in Canada all Indian people over 21 years of age had the right to vote in the 1962 general election. For the first time there was a way for them to express their likes and dislikes and exercise their democratic responsibilities under the franchise. That was an important step.
The previous administration also appointed a senator from the Indian people, so that again for the first time in Canada's history the Indians had a representative in parliament. If you look at the estimates of the various departments you will notice there was a dramatic increase in the moneys allocated to health, education, welfare and housing matters for Indian people. It is a basic principle that a cold, hungry, sick person is a second class citizen and that you must attack those evils before trying any other kind of rehabilitation.
The history of the Indian claims commission is a shoddy one, for which some of the responsibility must rest upon the minister's shoulders. On his head will rest the blame from the Indians, should we see a repetition of this history. Mention was first made of the establishment of an Indian claims commission in the throne speech of September 1962. This gave notice of legislation which would be brought in. At the same time, behind the scenes, the machinery for consulting the Indian people was set in motion. In the speech from the throne to the first session of the twenty sixth parliament in May, 1962, no mention is made of the Indian claims commission.
The government had changed, then.

The government had changed. But very early in the session a commitment

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
was made to proceed with the establishment. In August, 1963 I attended a convention in Winnipeg with the former minister, now the Minister of Justice. It was a convention of the national Indian council of Canada. The minister told the Indians who were assembled in Winnipeg from all parts of the country that legislation was to be introduced in the house before Christmas and that very soon the Indian people would have a commission to which they could bring all their claims and to which they could report all the injustices which everyone knows exist.
In November, 1963, when it became apparent there would be delay, I raised this matter in the House of Commons as reported in Hansard of November, 1963 on page 5898.
I recall that the minister of that day got excited when I suggested there had been a betrayal of the Indian people. He rose on a question of privilege to say that as superintendent general for Indian affairs he would not let these people down. At that time I said to the minister: If there is to be further delay, let the Indian people know about it, not just the members of this house, and tell them the new date by which it is expected the commission will be at work. If the minister were to do this, I said, he could retain the trust the Indian people had in him. And I can assure the minister from my meetings with Indian delegates, that they had trust in him. This was the suggestion I made to the minister in November-not to get excited and start protecting himself but to let the Indian people know of his plans.
The next page in this story of legislative indecision is to be found on page 319 of Hansard for February, 1964. By this time certain problems had arisen behind the scenes on the government side and there had been a change of minister. I am referring to page 319 of Hansard for February 27, 1964 where members will see that the present minister tells the house and, presumably, the Indian people of Canada, that the government does not intend to proceed with the legislation but intends to consult with the Indian bands. Almost a year after the government has taken office they intend to consult with the Indians as the only way of finding out what the Indian people really want. That is what the hon. gentleman said.
Well, in March of 1964, as hon. members will see if they refer to page 826 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration on the orders of the day how the consultations were going. He replied, in effect: They are going fine but we are still consulting with the Indian people; as soon as we get their advice we will boom ahead to set up this claims commission for them. And at the end of March, speaking on the minister's estimates, I gave the minister some advice-I did so because the portfolio had changed hands and I knew that the former minister might not have passed on the advice given him by members on this side of the house. I said this as reported in Hansard for March 13, 1964, at page 900:
The Indian claims commission holds tremendous promise for the Indian people of Canada. They are very keen on it. I have referred before to the efforts the previous minister made in dealing with the Indian people to assure them that the government was going to proceed with this commission,
I assure the present minister, as I did the past, that the Indian people are keen on the commission.
These are the pertinent words:
Do not betray their trust and do not, through inaction, allow their enthusiasm to wane and permit this commission to go the way of so many other projects.
Well, Mr. Chairman, nothing happened. The next episode I wish to put on record again is to be found reported at page 2760 of Hansard for April 30, 1964. I asked the minister on the orders of the day whether he could assure the house and the Indian people of Canada that he would proceed with the matter of the commission and introduce legislation at an early date. This was at the end of April. The minister replied, in effect, that he was still consulting with the Indian people; he still wanted to find out what they thought. But he intended to introduce the legislation during the second part Of the session.
After the recess.

Presumably it was to have been after our well earned summer recess.
The next entry to which I will call attention is reported at page 3683 of Hansard for Thursday, May 28. Again I asked the Minister, because I knew the federal provincial conference on Indian affairs was being postponed, whether this would have the effect of delaying a decision on the Indian claims commission until after October. The minister said in reply that it would not. It would not delay it, he said, because there was "no relation whatsoever between those two matters". That was at the end of May, 1964.
Now we come to August of 1964. The same minister. Here he is, this man of action, speaking in the house as reported at page 6861 of Hansard. He says this:
In keeping with our wish to consult the Indians on all matters of direct concern to them, the
8698	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indian claims Bill No. C-130, as introduced in the house on December 14 last, was sent in January to Indian bands, Indian organizations and others throughout the country.
The minister added that he had received some replies from the Indians and intended to give these close study. This was in August, 1964. Now he has consulted with the Indians and all that remains for him to do is to study the replies.
Let us see what happened in September, 1964. I refer, you, Mr. Chairman, to page 8387 of Hansard and to the question directed to the minister by the hon. member for Cariboo. The hon. member for Cariboo wonders how things are going with regard to the Indian claims commission and the minister says, in effect, that he has consulted with the Indians. He has obtained replies from them. Members will recall that the last time this matter was raised the hon. gentleman was going to study them. Well, he says on September 24 that he intends to consider the answers they have given. He has studied them, but he has not had time in which to consider them. However, he intends to do that very soon.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is a sorry mess the minister has got himself into. I say to him and to the government: If you don't want to help the Indian people, don't help them; but for God's sake do not hold out hope to the Indians and get them all stirred up by telling them that soon the terrible problems which have been theirs are to be solved-that soon, as the previous minister said, in effect, they would walk into the promised world of the white man. If you do not want to do anything, don't do it. But do not give us this nonsense which extends over 9,000 pages of Hansard. We asked the government to do this from the very beginning, but I ask the government not to lie to the Indian people. If it is not ready, then let the government tell us. Let them say to the Indian people: "We are sorry but this is a complicated matter and we are unable to make a decision on it now. We are sorry for you Indian people because we are going to do nothing for you". Every hon. member of this house is affected by this kind of delay, not just those of us with Indian people in our constituencies. Everyone in the house must take collective responsibility if a small group of people are betrayed.
Before the minister's estimates pass we on this side of the house want an answer to two questions. The first question is: "When is the government going to bring in the legislation on the Indian claims commission?


That should not be a difficult question to answer. The second question is: Will the government consider setting up some vehicle, say a committee hearing, where the Indian people can then take a look at this legislation? Because what I am afraid of is that this Indian claims commission, like so many other matters, is good for election after election. I can see the government bringing in the revised edition of the Indian claims commission legislation and the minister saying that, first of all, he must consult with the Indians and then consult with them some more, and then ask for advice, then for more time to study what they have said, and then he will want to consider that, and so on- just as he did the first time. Surely the questions I have put are not unreasonable ones.
I want to tell the minister why this is so important to the Indian people who happen to live in my part of the country. It may come as a surprise to some Canadians to know that there are no Indian reservations either in the Yukon or the Northwest Territories. There is good reason for this. Unfortunately, the reason, as I will unfold it, will be seen to be another chronicle of betrayal. The Indian people in the Yukon territory have had land, and I quote, "set aside" for them by order in council. Here again the history of what has happened to these parcels of land which were to be set aside is not good. Every time a government agency needed some of this land the order in council was merely revised. Surely the best example the committee has of this is when the government needed more land for the airport at Teslin in the Yukon. They simply took it away from property which was supposedly set aside for the Indians.
In the Northwest Territories even this much has not been done. Earlier I referred to the treaties signed with the Indian people in the north and which have never been lived up to. I have them here and they are interesting documents. We think the United States robbed the Indians when they bought Manhattan island, but surely there was no greater robbery than that which occurred in the signing of treaties Nos. 8 and 11. Treaty No. 8 took away nearly all of northern Alberta and part of the Northwest Territories from the Indians and gave it to the crown. That is an area of some 480,000 square miles and it was purchased in 1899 for $26,974 cash. Those who think the white man was not always crooked in his dealings with the Indians should read this treaty; they would be fascinated to learn of some of the other things

we gave to the Indians to make sure they had a good deal. For example each chief, after the signing of the treaty, was to receive a silver medal and a suitable flag-which is probably of more value than any of us thought was the case in those days. The following year and every third year thereafter each chief and head man was to receive a suitable suit of clothing. Here are some more of these "goodies":
-Her Majesty agrees to supply each chief of a band.. .for the use of that band 10 axes, five handsaws, five augers, one grindstone and the necessary files and whetstones.
That plus $26,000 cash, and you buy yourself 480,000 square miles of Alberta and the Northwest Territories.
I want to digress for a moment to mention another interesting matter. The other day the minister of northern affairs and some other hon. members of the house, including myself, were present when the Great Slave lake railway crossed the 60th parallel of latitude. That was an occasion for the great speech making, handshaking and self-congratulation amongst all of us because we had all done a brilliant job of driving the last spike. On going through these old treaties I noticed this remark made by the chief of the Chipewyan Indians at Fort Chipewyan, Alberta in 1899. This was what the commissioners said in the treaty:
We should add that the chief of the Chipewyans of Fort Chipewyan asked that the government should undertake to have a railway built into the country, as the cost of goods which the Indians require would be thereby cheapened and the prosperity of the country enhanced.
So really this suggestion came in 1899 from this old Indian chief. This shows in terms of the Great Slave lake railway that the Indians thought of this in 1899, the Liberals promised it in 1936 and the Conservatives built it in 1961. At any rate my point is that these treaties were signed with the Indian people of Canada's northland and were not lived up to, and for this reason they must have some sort of court or commission to which they can go.
The Indian people were promised basically two things. They were promised that their rights to hunt, trap and fish would not be curtailed; yet we all know that this is happening every day, not only in the north but all over Canada. The other thing they were promised-and this is where this point about there being no reservations comes in-was one square mile of land for every five Indian people who signed the treaty. This was true in the treaty signed in 1899 and it was true in
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the second treaty signed in 1922 with the rest of the Indian people of the Northwest Territories, but this land in fact was never set aside for the Indian people; and so the two things promised them in return for peacefully allowing the white man into their country were never advanced to them. Because of that there are no reservations. No one in the Northwest Territories, to my knowledge, wants the government to set up Indian reservations at this stage, but everyone wants the government to live up to its obligations, to renegotiate the treaties and to make good the commitments undertaken in 1899 and 1922.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest to the minister that in addition to getting on with this legislation he has been dangling before us for so many months he give consideration to setting up a national advisory Indian council, much in the same way the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has a national religious advisory council. More and more is required a vehicle for consultation between the government and the Indian people. I suggest that in view of the tremendous changes being made almost daily in the programs which the minister has under his department this would be invaluable. Indian peoples could be represented on it and we could consult them in a meaningful way, and thus overcome the basic obstacle of mistrust which I suggest to the minister is coming between himself and the efficient administration of his department.
In resuming my place, Mr. Chairman, I should like to terminate my remarks with a word of gratitude on behalf of the members of this house for the fine work that has been done by some of the old hands of the Indian affairs branch who have retired in the last several years. Most of us knew these men who served many years in that branch during a difficult period of administration in Canada, and who guided the Indian people as far as the position they now occupy.
There is now a new look in the Indian affairs branch, which is long overdue. The staff is new and there is a new spirit, and all of us welcome these changes. We are happy to hear of the creation of an assistant deputy minister's post for the former director of the Indian affairs branch, Mr. Battle. We are happy not only because he personally has been appointed to this post, but because this appointment gives further recognition to the important part the Indian affairs branch plays in the work of this department.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
