Mr, Chairman, at this
stage of the consideration of the estimates of the Indian affairs, I want to address a few remarks to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) about the small reservation of Pointe Bleue located in my constituency. Further to an article published in L'Etoile du Lac, a district newspaper, on September 17 last, entitled "On the war path", I have advised the minister of the small revolt that is coming on within the Pointe Bleue reservation in connection with certain methods of a certain company.
I put several questions to the minister and I told him that I believed that he was completely unaware of certain things that were going on in the Pointe Bleue reservation, in connection with the Hudson's Bay Company.
I will not read the letter as I have only ten minutes at my disposal, but further to my letter, the minister answered that he had sent investigators. And it is on this point that I should like to call the minister's attention. The investigators he has sent are precisely those we did not want. In fact, it is the same as if we were asking for an inquiry into a theft and the thieves were sent in to investigate. That is the situation I want to put before the minister. I have no grudge whatsoever against him. I merely want to throw some light on the matter and help him do justice to the Indians.
Therefore we shall examine in a general manner what is happening today on the Pointe Bleue reservation, and particularly the causes of this unrest. I will even suggest some solutions to this problem. As I said a moment ago, I wish to warn the minister before this report is received.
As I requested in my letter, the minister must study the role which was played and which is still being played by the Hudson's Bay Company in the Pointe Bleue reservation. This English firm is the only one established on the reservation. It is not there for the sake of the Indians; it is there to do business, and probably very profitable business because it has not been facing any competition for three quarters of a century. If the minister would only visit that reservation, he would see and hear all kinds of things.
For instance, it is said that during the years the company controlled the economy, not a single Indian dared stand up against it. Indeed, none of them could afford to.
You hear about winters during which the only rations issued to the Indians by the com-


pany were flour, salted pork, beans, coarse salt, third quality molasses and oatmeal. In fact, whenever a person needed a little bit of cereal, powdered milk or something else for his children, he had to trade his rations of oatmeal and salted pork with someone else to get it. It is said that pregnant women had to pass whole winters eating only oatmeal, three times a day. Perhaps it would have been too costly for the company to feed those people somewhat like human beings.
In addition to supplying them third rate goods, it bought Indian products at ridiculous prices and paid the Indians in oatmeal and flour. This is the kind of stories one hears when one takes the trouble to mix with those people.
In the last few years a number of Indians, whose patience was at an end, risked all their savings in an attempt to provide better service to their fellow citizens. From that time a few little shops were opened and sold all the goods found in ordinary groceries. The Hudson's Bay Company was not long in retorting. From that day it sold all the goods it had never dared to put on sale and, moreover, it cut its prices to such an extent that they were even lower than those asked by Indian merchants. The company even went so far as to organize a delivery system.
Today the Indians are capable of having a market of their own and if we encourage the Indian merchants by offering them the same privileges as those which were tacitly or effectively granted the Hudson's Bay Company, I am almost certain that it will be to the advantage of the entire tribe.
At the present time the Indian merchants are unable to deal with any banking or financial institution. Hence the unequal strugr gle against a company that has all the financial powers on its side.
I am therefore of the opinion that if the minister, in conjunction with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), were to set up a federal finance organization serving only the Indians but having some contact outside the reservation, he would put the struggle on a more equal footing. The lack of such an organization seems to enable the company to keep the population of the reserve under its financial domination.
I am told that these days in order to subsist, the Indian must have a charge account with the Hudson's Bay Company. If he wants to work for an engineer or a prospector, he must report to the company's office and sign a slip authorizing the company's

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
employees to get his pay and administer it as they see fit.
It seems that the company carries things even further, going so far as to collect almost all allowance cheques directly from the post office. In my opinion, this way of doing things is quite unfair to the Indians.
For these reasons and many others I do not have the time to mention at this point, some Indians assisted by a large number of their fellow members anxious to free themselves of foreign influence, have launched a market in order to protect the Indians. In 1961, when the band council renewed for ten years the company's lease, it did so on one condition, which I want to mention: that the company could not develop its trade. This is, Mr. Chairman, what the Indian merchants want, supported unanimously by the band council. Nevertheless after three years the company wants to develop its trade.
The minister was told that there was a lease but without any mention that this lease included the specific condition which I just mentioned. This is the main reason that prompts me to call these facts to the attention of the minister.
When I am told that arrangements have been made for a meeting between representatives of the Hudson's Bay Company and the Indian people, I say that the meeting took place with representatives of the Hudson's Bay Company but not with those of the Indian merchants on the reservation. There seems to have been a secret meeting of some members of the band council, even using the secretary of the reservation agent instead of the official secretary of the band council.
The Indian merchants were ignored and the representatives of the Quebec office and of the agency had a private meeting with the company.
I think that the Indians are living in a tragic period and that the minister must make the necessary clean up. People always took pleasure in hanging fear, like a sword of Damocles, over the head of the Indian authorities, through political, monetary or social threats, for the sole purpose of making Indian authorities renounce their first decisions, in order to show that the Indians cannot administer themselves.
The time has come to end such a ridiculous situation and to guarantee to the Indians their commercial freedom, their freedom of action within the limits of their reservation.
I am sure that a serious investigation carried out by officials other than those of the Quebec office or the reservation agency,
will show that the Indians can administer themselves and that if the minister will give them the necessary assistance, they could almost be self-sufficient instead of being citizens that the government pays for doing nothing.
At this time I recall an observation made to me by a good Indian to whom I pointed out that he received a social allowance. He answered: "Well yes, but what is most demoralizing is waiting for the meagre allowance without having the right to work."
What surprised me, Mr. Chairman, was to note that the small pension of $15 which an Indian pensioner receives must be reduced if he works one, two or three days.
If the minister were to get together with the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), he would see, I think, that he has a magnificent opportunity to apply usefully the ARDA program, and thus to foster the agricultural rehabilitation of the whole reserve.
Substantial loans might be granted to the band council to develop the tourist industry at Pointe Bleue.
We spend more than $30 million which produces no result, while every year thousands of tourists must turn back because there are practically no accommodations on the reservation. Yet the most wonderful tourist attraction in Lake St. John is at Pointe Bleue.
I am positive that if the government wanted to make an effort and spend a little of that money to improve that area, tremendous results would ensue; besides creating many jobs for the Indians of the reservation, it would enable them to promote their handicraft with the tourists who would certainly be attracted by those improvements. This would also help to make the Indian proud again, for he, too, would like to be able to say that he is an asset in the Canadian economy; in this way, he would be able to live a happier life, because he would have a greater awareness of the importance of his actions and his contribution within the reservation.
Pointe Bleue has all that is needed to make it a tourist attraction. The only condition is to give the required opportunities and encouragement to its people. The government has the duty to take action before the war axe is dug up, because wars were always brought on by injustice piling up.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest, as I am sure other members did, to the remarks of the
8702	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration hon. member who spoke on behalf of the Conservative party, and while listening to him I came to the conclusion that the present minister is perhaps at least as bad as if not worse than Hon. Ellen Fairclough, when she held that particular office.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: She is not here. Don't attack people not here.

I am not mentioning that because she is not here. It is not my fault she is not here; someone else had a hand in that. In any event, the former prime minister decided she was relatively useless in Indian Affairs and moved her from that post to something else before the election took place. I only make that comment in reply to that just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in a low voice.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will make it louder then. It is a scurrilous remark.
Get up and say that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will get up and say it. On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think it is very much out of order for a member of this house to attack a former minister of the crown who is not present here, and I object to that procedure.

It is unfortunate that the member who just raised that point of order was not the minister of citizenship and immigration himself, because one could perhaps make a comment about his activities in the cabinet. I have no intention of becoming embroiled in a crossfire with him in particular.
Why did you start it?

It will be recalled that last year when the present Minister of Justice held the portfolio of citizenship and immigration the house was in a mood to expedite the passage of the estimates because they had been held over for some period of time and there was a desire to complete the business before parliament in order to get back on a more regular basis in the consideration of parliamentary matters and government expenditures. Accordingly, many hon. members refrained from making suggestions and criticisms with regard to the operation of the Indian affairs branch, and accepted the bland assurances of the former minister that something worth while was going to be done. So far, however, we have not seen any great example of the desire and the speed with which Indian affairs should be tackled.
I have been asked by a number of bands at home, and there are a number from which


difficulties and problems, but this is only nibbling away at the periphery of the difficulties because these are but isolated instances.
The record of successive governments is black and sterile. It is disgraceful. Generally speaking, Indian people by and large have been trusting over the years. If government has told them something they, perhaps with some naivete, have believed government. If the Indian agent has come and told them something is going to happen they have believed the Indian agent. But their patience and trust are wearing pretty thin. We should no longer permit ourselves the luxury of an annual invasion into the Indian affairs branch in parliament in this way, as we come to question the estimates of that particular branch. This is not good enough.
In the future we cannot permit ourselves to allow a situation to exist which would require the kind of speech the hon. member for Northwest Territories made today, and to have to say the kind of things which my own feelings and conscience force me to say. This is no longer good enough. There is a great and growing resentment among Indian people all across Canada, in all Indian villages and reserves. There is a growing resentment among native people who, for a variety of reasons, left the reserves and went to live in urbanized and semi-urbanized areas-incidentally living on the fringe of them because that is the only place they are accepted.
There is much talk among many people about digging up the tomahawk they buried many years ago, because they have come to believe that the trust and faith they placed in the words of government are not worth placing any longer. The older people still continue to fight as they can. In their council meetings they still continue to caution the younger generation about doing things in the normal way. They still continue to advise the younger generation that they should air their complaints and grievances in meetings of council with the Indian agent, that they should present their demands and grievances by way of resolutions, passed and channelled through the Indian agent, the commissioners and the directors up some place to the top, and eventually hope some communication will filter back to the band so that they will know what happened to their grievances.
But the younger people have had a taste of the non-Indian society. Those in their teens and twenties have had better opportunities for education than their parents, and having found it necessary to move away from the

reserve in order to work, are finding and searching out the ways of the non-Indian and are discovering from a little taste of this type of society of the non-Indian that they want more of it, and they are wondering why it is denied them.
They will not be content with the mere passing of resolutions in council meetings. They will not be content with sitting around a council fire discussing things among themselves and with their elders and advisers. They will not be content with listening to being put off by the Indian agent. They will not be content with having their grievances lost in the mass of red tape in the Indian affairs branch.
They are a rising group of people. Their population is expanding tremendously. They are a volatile group of people when they get going. Mr. Minister, you should appreciate this, coming from the province you do and having the racial origin you have. You should appreciate that what the native Indian people are seeking is almost identical with what the French people are seeking. You, with your background and your understanding of your own culture, should appreciate what this means and should be able to move with great speed to cope with the Indian's problem.
I do not envisage-at least I hope to heaven it never comes to this-that we will have an uprising of our native people, such as has been the case in other countries. But mark my words, it could happen, and the spark which will set it off will be a continuation of the practice of the past. This will be the thing which will allow that feeling of resentment to burst into flame and perhaps consume what sociological relations we have with our native people.
Please, Mr. Minister, do not take these words personally as applying to you. Do not take the words that are directed by Indian bands as applying to your government exclusively. To the members of the Indian affairs branch I say, do not take these words as applying individually and personally to you. Do not take the resentment of native people as being aimed in your direction. These feelings of resentment are directed at our society, at successive governments, and they are the outgrowth of many years of delay, of lies, of distortions of all sorts, and of the most degrading activities people can engage in. Fairly shortly we will be facing the time of truth.
There are many other things I wish to go into detail on, when we get further into the estimates. At this stage I can only echo the utterances of the older people of the
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration villages I know personally, and say they are praying as they never prayed before that something worth while will be done.

I shall not take up too much
time of the committee; but I wish to deal with the announcement made by the minister in replying to questions I put to him on September 30 last, as recorded at pages 8586, 8587 and 8588 of Hansard for that day. The minister made an announcement on that occasion with respect to the negotiations which are now being conducted between officials on behalf of the federal government and officials on behalf of the provinces, to transfer jurisdiction of educational and social welfare matters to the provinces, and I use that word "jurisdiction" advisedly, even though a rather hairy distinction is made by the minister and others opposite between it and the word "responsibility."
Referring to the forthcoming federal-provincial conference the minister said, as recorded at page 8586 of Hansard:
As it so happens, we shall be discussing measures that would enable the provinces to extend a number of provincial services to the Indians, on condition the federal government grant compensation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Would the hon. member repeat the date?

The date is September 30, and the page is 8586. The committee will remember the discussions which took place concerning the proposals of the federal government to transfer jurisdiction over the Eskimo people of Quebec to the government of that province. The minister knows that the Eskimo people are Indians by virtue of a supreme court decision of 1939, and for purposes of the Indian Act they come under federal jurisdiction. I suggest to the minister that regardless of his own personal assessment of federal legislation and its constitutionality in this regard, any transfer of jurisdiction over the Indian or Eskimo people from the federal government to any other authority is ultra vires under the terms of section 91(24) of the British North America Act which places squarely upon the shoulders of the federal government responsibility or jurisdiction in this regard. Any exercise of a purported authority to transfer control, jurisdiction or responsibility, whatever the minister chooses to call it, over the Indian or the Eskimo people of Canada to a provincial authority is an abrogation of the power expressly given to the parliament of Canada, as opposed to the executive, by section 91(28) of the British North America Act.
8706	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
It is said in answer to this that the Indian Act gives sufficient power to the executive to transfer control and responsibility to the provinces by process of agreement. I suggest to the minister that he re-examine the legal assessment he may have placed on this situation in the light of what I have to say. If the Indian Act does purport to give this power to the executive, then to that extent the Indian Act is ultra vires and in conflict with section 91(24) of the British North America Act which places such power in the hands of the parliament of Canada. Unless and until section 91(24) is amended, the purported exercise of that power by the executive is wrong and ultra vires.
What is really happening here, one may conjecture, is that what the resources minister of Quebec has failed to get by the front door he is now getting by the back door. As a result of the pressure put on the government, and of the publicity given at the time the subject was raised, he did not succeed in getting control over the education and social welfare of the Eskimo population of Quebec as he wished to do. This is just another way of appeasing Mr. Levesque and his friends. There is no difference between that case and the considerations raised by the transfer of jurisdiction or responsibility with respect to the Indian people of that province. An attempt has been made to draw a nice distinction between those terms by the minister and by others on the government benches. But the distinction is not valid, because if responsibility were to be transferred in any other way than by an amendment to the British North America Act, which would be constitutionally proper, it would necessarily include the transfer of jurisdiction over the people concerned and no amount of nice definitions can alter that plain fact.
The Indian people of Canada were guaranteed as a minority certain fundamental rights by the treaty of Paris and the royal proclamation made thereunder in 1763. Those rights are perpetuated by the inclusion in the British North America Act of section 91(24), any any attempt to abrogate them would be a travesty of justice. I believe the minister and his advisers should take a hard second look at this whole question.
Regardless of the intention of the federal government with respect to this matter the assurances which have been given to the house by the Prime Minister and by the minister himself are insufficient. The minister and the Prime Minister grandly say that before any decision is taken the Indian people them-


selves-and I presume he intends also to include the Eskimo people-will be consulted. In all fairness to those who are most concerned, the consultation which is required here is consultation in advance, because the Indian people themselves may have some ideas, and extremely valid ideas, as to whether or not they wish jurisdiction to be transferred at all. They should be consulted in advance, not bandied about like chattels, to recall a phrase which was used by one speaker on this side of the house.
I do not know whether I am correctly interpreting the remarks made by the minister as reported on page 8586 of Hansard for September 30 but I was surprised to see this statement with respect to consultation before transfer:
I can assure the two hon. members and the entire house that the federal government will not make any major decision during this parliament before consulting the Indians themselves, as they are the first concerned in all these measures and, all the more so, the provincial authorities.
I say this to the minister that it should be "all the more so the Indian people" in order of importance, surely. The consultations to be held should be consultations with the people directly concerned, that is with the Indian people. Then once the minister has established their views and conveyed them to his colleagues in the cabinet-and the Indians may reject outright any proposal for transfer, in which case that should be the end of the matter-once their views have been ascertained, that is the time to evolve a policy which might be discussed with provincial authorities.
Five o'clock.

I did not say it.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. R. Southam (Moose Mountain) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MORATORIUM ON ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-57, to amend the Railway Act (abandonment moratorium).
He said: Mr. Speaker, my first words on rising this afternoon to speak to the second reading of Bill No. C-57 is to express both on behalf of myself and I am sure on behalf of other hon. members our regret that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is ill and confined to hospital. I am sure we all wish him a speedy recovery and look forward to having him back in the house at an early date. It was my hope he would be here this afternoon to listen to the principle which I will espouse in speaking to this bill. I might say that I first introduced it to the house on June 7, 1963 as Bill No. C-70, but it was so far down the order paper that it did not come up for second reading last year. Consequently I had the pleasure of reintroducing it in the house this year as Bill No. C-57 and it was read for the first time on February 20, 1964.
I should like to give a brief explanation to the house of the bill, and I think I could do no better than to refer to my previous remarks when introducing the bill last year, which remarks are to be found at page 771 of Hansard for Friday, June 7, 1963. At that time I said:
Mr. Speaker, the magnitude of the problem of railway abandonment is becoming apparent from the large mass of applications being directed to the board of transport commissioners based on recommendations of the MacPherson royal commission on transportation. These abandonments are estimated to affect between 4,300 and 8,600 miles of branch lines. About 4,000 to 5,000 miles of this total is in the three prairie provinces, and 2,000 miles is in Saskatchewan.
The purpose of this bill is to declare a moratorium of five years on all applications respecting rail abandonment accepted and granted by the board of transport commissioners so that private persons, rural and urban municipalities, primary producers, industries, businesses, elevator companies, wheat pools, labour organizations, the motor transport and pipe line industries and all others which may be adversely affected may plan well in advance before the abandonment actually takes place, in this way alleviating as far as possible the social and economic upheaval that may occur in many communities, especially those in rural areas.
Railway Act
At that time I said I hoped the bill would receive widespread support not only in the house but across Canada, and I might say this was the reaction it received. I had correspondence coming in from a wide area which suggested that the principle involved in the bill was receiving wide support and sympathy.
I might also say that my reason for introducing the bill was because of an experience I had in the matter of the Reston-Wolseley rail abandonment which came before the board of transport commissioners in 1959. This Reston-Wolseley line commenced in the constituency of Brandon-Souris, went across my riding of Moose Mountain and into the riding of Qu'Appelle, a distance of 122 miles. I am sure hon. members realize that this abandonment was quite a shock to the people in that area, as it affected quite a large community. At that time I debated the abandonment in this house and brought forward facts and figures, as well as appearing before the board of transport commissioners to make the plea that the abandonment should not take place until the MacPherson royal commission report was brought in and proper legislation enacted. However the board of transport commissioners in their wisdom saw fit to concur in the abandonment of this line.
In this particular case, although the abandonment was very serious to the people concerned, it was not as serious as might have been the case owing to the fact that the Canadian National line ran adjacent, almost parallel a short distance away, to the Reston-Wolseley line for quite a large extent of its coverage. Therefore the shock was not as severe as it otherwise might have been. Nevertheless it was still bad enough to create a great deal of concern among the various people affected, as I outlined in my explanation when I introduced my previous bill, and as a result I felt that we as members of parliament should take a serious look at the present Railway Act.
I should like at this point to read for the benefit of the house the explanation of this present bill. It is to amend section 168 of the Railway Act by adding thereto the following subsection:
(2) Every approval when given by the board stands appealed to the governor in council for a time expiring five years from the day approval is given or until an order of the governor in council is sooner made to confirm, vary or rescind such approval.
The explanatory notes continue as follows:
The section was first enacted...by amendment to the act in 1932-33, c. 47, s.l. Prior to that year

Railway Act
railway companies could under common law, unless there were a contractual or statutory duty to continue operations, abandon the operation of the whole or any part of their lines without the approval of the board. Between 1922 and 1933 the board of transport commissioners, in a series of decisions, consistently upheld this common law right of the railways. In 1933 parliament, while recognizing this common law right of the railways, restricted the liberty of action of the companies in exercising this right by providing the companies must have the approval of the board. The board takes into consideration the interests of the company and the public. The section was a remedy to one of the economic pressures of the depression. It was not conceived as a remedy for the pressures that urge mass abandonment today. The board has held that the section gives no right to compensation by industries, primary producers, or others who are seriously affected by the deprivation of transport, or to railway workers who suffer financial loss by change of residence or earlier retirement.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel in view of the fact that there is before the house today Bill No. C-120 this proposed amendment to the Railway Act is very timely.
One of the recourses which we had to this particular act as it now applies was section 53, and I want to refer to that section. It reads as follows:
The governor in council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order that the governor in council may make with respect thereto is binding upon the board and upon all parties.
In 1961 the residents affected by the proposed abandonment of the Reston-Wolseley line made an application to the governor in council for alleviation or assistance in respect of that abandonment. Their application was given consideration, and the abandonment was held in abeyance for 30 days, but it finally went through.
There is one other alternative, although I do not think it is of much benefit to the people involved. Individuals can ask for the retention of a branch line after an application has been made for abandonment, provided they can find a legal or technical reason. These individuals can go to the Supreme Court of Canada for relief, but I do not think that actually happens very often. As a consequence, this alternative does not provide much assistance to people affected by rail line abandonments.
My bill asking for this rail line abandonment moratorium should be considered very seriously by the government. The knowledge that this principle was being considered

seriously by the government would lessen the concern of thousands of people across Canada who are today faced with this abandonment situation. I think there will still be grounds for concern even after Bill No. C-120 has been discussed, considered, perhaps amended and passed. The government should give serious consideration to the suggestion that the principles contained in my bill should be included in the legislative measures proposed by the government in respect of rationalization or rail line abandonment.
Many other things are of concern to the people of Canada in respect of rail line abandonment. Some of them are as follows; the abandonment of approximately 4,500 to 8,500 miles of line to which I referred a few moments ago, spiralling freight rate increases, heavy increases in the cost of marketing farm grain, captive freight rate areas, great lack of railway passenger service, widespread concern of railway workers, and social and economic upheaval of both urban and rural individuals living adjacent to proposed line abandonments.
In an attempt to substantiate my statements about this concern, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read from the front page of the Western Producer of October 1, 1964. The headline is "Legislation on branch line abandonment totally inadequate, says pool president". The reference in that headline is to the Saskatchewan wheat pool, which is the largest wheat pool handling grain in western Canada. Mr. Charles Gibbings, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, is one of the most qualified individuals in western Canada to speak in respect of the handling of grain and for those individuals who are seriously affected by proposed rail line abandonments. This article carries a subheading "West facing transportation crisis", and at page 38 reads as follows:
Applications to abandon branch lines totalling nearly 2,000 miles of track serving 260 communities are on file with the board of transport commissioners. The lines serve 547 country elevators with a total capacity of more than 39 million bushels. The branches are shown on the map above.
The abandonment applications have been filed by the railways over a period of two years. Consideration has been held up pending the introduction of legislation to deal with, railway matters. Most of the applications on file were made by Canadian National in response to appeals from farm organizations and the government for information to show the scope of the branch line problem. Canadian Pacific has not committed itself on its overall plans, filing only on a piece-by-piece basis.
Legislation to deal with branch line abandonment was introduced by the government September 14 as part of a transportation policy arising from the report of the MacPherson commission. Saskatch-

ewan wheat pool and other farm organizations have expressed grave concern at terms of the bill dealing with branch lines. The pools have indicated intention to request far reaching amendments.
Mr. Speaker, I could say a good deal more in explanation of this bill but I think I have placed substantial information on the record this afternoon to give something more than a general outline. I am sure other hon. members wish to speak in support of this bill.
Before resuming my seat I would again urge the government to consider the principles of Bill C-57, so that when any application by either the C.N.R., the C.P.R. or any other railway company in Canada for the abandonment of a branch line has been approved, before such abandonment takes place there will be a five year moratorium allowing the urban and rural residents an opportunity to adjust their plans so as to avoid the severe impact of such an abandonment.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MORATORIUM ON ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not usual for a minister to speak during private members' hour, but I have taken the trouble to refresh my memory and I know it is quite proper to speak at this time. References to this effect will be found in paragraph 748 of Beauchesne's third edition, and on page 581 of Bourinot's. In any event, I felt I owed a duty to this house to bring to its attention during the consideration of this bill certain relevant matters.
The bill itself is an attempt by an hon. member to put forward a piece of legislation, by way of an amendment to the Railway Act, to assist mainly in protecting the interests of grain producers and other affected parties in western Canada, where a great many branch railway lines will possibly be the subject of applications for abandonment.
The hon. member I am sure will understand if I suggest that there should be a reservation as to the figures he used in respect of the mileage involved. Both this government and the previous one invited the railways to file applications for every proposed abandonment in the three prairie provinces. In light of the premise upon which those applications were made, it will be seen that the total proposed mileage subject to abandonment is an over-inflated figure.
Having expressed that reservation, Mr. Speaker, I must admit that the problem is a very real and serious one, and I understand and appreciate the concern of the residents 20220-551i
Railway Act
in those affected areas. Without any desire to be technical, I respectfully suggest that the bill itself does not do what the hon. member wishes to be done, and if I may be allowed to develop my remarks along that line for a few moments I should like to do so.
The bill itself merely allows the appeal of every case to the governor in council, and I suggest that authority already exists. Anybody can appeal a case now to the governor in council under the existing legislation. The objection to this form of appeal under which every case would be automatically appealed is that it would change the whole scheme of the present board of transport commissioners legislation whereby they perform a quasijudicial function, and make that function one performed subject to review in every instance by the governor in council and put an inordinate work load on the governor in council without the governor in council in turn developing adequate machinery to deal with those appeals. I would submit that the legislation before us is defective on that point.
What is needed to deal with this matter is dealt with rather fully in Bill No. C-120, the bill based on the MacPherson royal commission report and now before the house for consideration. Any changes that should be made in the part of that bill dealing with this subject should properly be made by way of amendment to that bill at the committee stage. There is nothing different in principle, so it would not involve rejection of the bill. If the point of argument made by the hon. member is valid, that would be a matter to be raised by way of amendment to the particular clauses on this subject when Bill No. C-120, an act to amend the Railway Act, is before the house.
As is obvious to hon. members, that bill is a very long and complicated one. I expect it will take some considerable examination at the committee stage and I would expect that there would be a good deal of discussion on this very vital point. But I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that clause 7 of that bill provides for adding a whole new part to the Railway Act, that new part to be headed "Abandonment of Lines or Operations, Uneconomic Branch Lines", which is the very subject matter causing concern. There is of course legislative provision for setting up a rationalization authority to deal with this whole question. That rationalization authority, after a line is found to be uneconomic and eligible for abandonment under the present concept of what makes a branch rail line eligible for

Railway Act
abandonment, is given jurisdiction to deal with the subject of abandonment, the time of abandonment and to make quite extensive orders.
I do not want to argue the proposition in detail here, but it will be seen that the rationalization authority has the kind of jurisdiction that permits it to look at the services in the whole region affected by the abandonment of a particular branch line or branch lines, and it has the kind of authority required to permit it to deal, not with each individual application by itself but with each application in relation to the effect on possible patronage that abandonment of railway service will have in the area, or in relation to other applications for abandonment, so that the whole result from the decisions made will be a rational system of railway lines. That is the approach to the problem.
The criteria established for the authority in reaching its conclusions will be found on page 7 of the bill in these words:
.. .the authority shall fix the earliest such date or dates consistent with the public interest and for that purpose shall have regard to all matters that appear to the authorities to be relevant including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing-
Hon. members will note the breadth of the criteria that the authority must apply in making a decision on what is consistent with the public interest.
- (a) the alternative transportation facilities available or likely to be available to the area served by the line;
(b)	the period of time reasonably required for the purpose of adjusting any facilities, wholly or in part dependant on the services provided by the line, with the least disruption to the economy of the area served by such line;
(c)	the probable effect on other lines or other carriers of the abandonment of the line or of the abandonment of any segments of the line at different dates;
(d)	any rule prescribed by the authority for the orderly processing of applications for the abandonment of lines in the area served by the line or in surrounding areas;
(e)	the feasibility of maintaining the line or any segment thereof as an operating line by changes in the method of operation;
(f)	the feasibility of maintaining the line or any segment thereof as an operating line in the system of another rail carrier by the purchase or lease of the line to another railway company or otherwise; and
(g)	the probable future transportation needs of the area served by the line.
In other words, the government legislation before the house for its consideration and decision does attempt to deal with this subject in a broad, comprehensive way by creating

an authority having wide powers and having authority based on serving the public interest which is defined in the widest possible way in that bill. If the point raised by the hon. member is valid, and I acknowledge at once the concern of farmers and other people engaged in the whole economy of the three prairie provinces particularly, I am under obligation to point out to hon. members that the whole subject will be before them when the government legislation is being examined. While I cannot speak for the committee, which has jurisdiction over how it conducts its own business, I think it must be readily apparent to all hon. members, and a reasonable presumption, that the appropriate public bodies throughout these provinces will appear before the committee. I have reference to the elevator operators, the grain growers' organizations, the relevant farm organizations and representatives of the provincial governments as well, I presume. Therefore the whole subject will be examined rather thoroughly there.
If the provisions in the government's bill are inadequate, then any changes along the lines suggested would not be a matter for separate amendment of the Railway Act by way of a separate bill, but can only properly be a matter for amendment to the clauses on the subject, when those clauses are before the appropriate committee for consideration. I thought I ought to make that point and I thank hon. members for hearing me out on this matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MORATORIUM ON ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
I want to make that point clear. I realize what the situation is under the existing law, but my amendment suggests that if and when people affected by an aban-

donment make application to the board of transport commissioners under section 53, the board would automatically have to allow a five year moratorium before the abandonment became effective.
The whole principle of this bill is to hold this in abeyance in order to alleviate the shock. I went on to refer then to my experience in connection with the abandonment of the Reston-Wolseley line. As soon as the application was accepted by the board of transport commissioners under section 53, they wrapped up this line and there was an economic and social shock to the area. Under this amendment I am suggesting today, and which I think should get serious consideration from the government when they consider Bill No. C-120, after rationalization and everything else had been considered, when the abandonment of any piece of line had been finally considered there should be a five year moratorium applied to it. This is the new concept.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MORATORIUM ON ABANDONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to speak on Bill No. C-57. The minister has said there is a Bill No. C-120 on the order paper which will be discussed later, but I should like to speak about matters with which 1 am very familiar, namely railway abandonments and the effect they will have on my particular province. I know that should this railway abandonment plan go through it will affect a great number of farmers. It will affect not only a great number of farmers but it will affect communities, towns and even villages and hamlets. At the present time there will be approximately 1,746 miles of railway line abandoned, and when you take into consideration the fact that 235 elevators will be abandoned-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MORATORIUM ON ABANDONMENT
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Why does he use these figures, giving in absolute terms the mileage pf lines that will be abandoned, when he does not even know whether or not applications for the abandonment of these lines will be proceeded with?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MORATORIUM ON ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
The reason I know these are the figures is because the railways have indicated them, and the towns and villages that are affected have all set up retention commit-ties which have made representation to the provincial government. That is why I mention so many miles being abandoned, because

these places have secured the figures from the railway companies.
These 235 elevators would take in possibly 64 million bushels of grain in any one crop year. If the railways are abandoned these elevators will not operate any more, and farmers who produce grain will be confronted with much higher expense delivering grain to elevators.
The Crowsnest pass agreement provides a stipulated rate for the delivery of grain, but if a farmer has to haul his grain 40 or 50 miles to a station, then the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rate will be almost useless to him. That is why the farmers in the three western provinces are so concerned about rail line abandonment. If the lines are abandoned there will be the extra cost of delivering grain to the elevators. The farmers will also suffer capital losses because the value of their farms will not be so high when they are located 20, 30 or 40 miles from a grain elevator. Further, the value of the towns affected will not be as high as they are at present. These are the reasons why retention committees have been set up in the three western provinces. I am aware railway rationalization legislation is being introduced, but I think now is the time for us to stress these points. If the railway lines are abandoned it will be the greatest disaster ever to strike the three prairie provinces.
The other day when we were discussing immigration the minister said he intended to encourage immigrants who were well educated and trained. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) then pointed out that his area could accommodate an additional 5 million people to open up the country, and pointed out that the Pine Point railway gives that opportunity for opening it up.
The minister has said that all these matters pertaining to railway abandonment should be directed to a committee for consideration, where witnesses and representatives of the railways could be called, and all these things discussed around the table to see whether railway abandonment is necessary or not. I point out that since the railways themselves have always been opposed to the Crowsnest pass agreement, by abandonment of so many lines they think they would not lose so much money by hauling grain under the Crowsnest pass arrangement.
That is all I have to say at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) has

shown an interest in this important subject.
I would point out that those of us who come from areas that are badly in need of industrial development are much concerned with the question of railway policy.
I see the smiling and benign countenance of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) in the chamber, and I wish to say there should be some co-ordination between railway policies and the general policies of those of us on this side of the house with respect to industrial development, and its encouragement in those areas that have fallen behind the rest of the country. I do not think we can divorce from the question of railway policy the motivations and directions of the Department of Industry toward industrialization.
The Department of Industry is devoted to the encouragement of industrial development. It has promoted measures such as the designated area legislation, and its new branch, the area development agency, is devoted to encouraging industrial development in areas of slow growth. For that reason I do not think the department can operate without giving some thought to the government's railway policy, because one essential for industrial development in slow growth areas is that those areas should have adequate railway service. We shall not achieve industrial development, no matter how wise or far seeing are the policies of the Department of Industry, if railway policies are such as to divest designated areas of railway service.
Because of this I am pleased to note the government has already introduced Bill No. C-120, which indicates very broad thinking in this area of railway line abandonment. It certainly leaves room and scope for the thought I have in mind, which is that the whole question of railways should be correlated to the need for the distribution of industries across our broad land to a far greater degree than has been the case.
I note that Bill No. C-120 proposes to a large degree the implementation of the findings of the MacPherson commission, and while I have some sympathy with the aims of Bill No. C-57 I personally feel the implementation of the entire ambit of the findings of the MacPherson commission, as envisaged by Bill C-120, is preferable to a hodgepodge, a piecemeal approach to the problem.
I am particularly pleased to support the general premise that the findings of the MacPherson commission should be embodied in government legislation, by reason of the fact that the commission was headed by M. A. MacPherson, who has the very outstanding
Railway Act
and distinguishing mark of having been once rejected by his party as leader of that party. I think this is a mark to be proudly worn. I, too, am sorry the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is not here to consider this bill, which has some bearing on Bill C-120 which he himself introduced. We were all extremely sorry to learn of his illness and I was pleased to hear the sponsor of this bill wish him well. I should like to inform the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) who is always concerned about the well-being of the Minister of Transport that I am instructed on reliable authority that while he is in hospital his white flowing robes will be cleaned and will be purged of any stain which remains thereon from the pipe line. I know the hon. member will be very pleased to hear this, as he has been concerned about it in the past.
I think we should consider Bill C-120 in its entirety to determine whether or not the matter which is dealt with in the bill before us is not considered in a far broader way and in a far more satisfactory way, in my humble submission, in the former measure. We know that in clause 6 of Bill C-120, section 168 of the act is amended to cover the entire policy of the abandonment of railway lines. A number of clauses, from clause 6 onward, are concerned with this whole question of the abandonment of rail lines and its effect upon the economy-and not only upon the economy of the railway companies. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) that up to the present time the difficulty attached to these hearings-and I have taken some part in them in the past-is that the commissioners have had to consider the economic position of the railway companies as the main criterion with respect to applications for abandonment. Those of us who represent constituencies in which economic development is badly needed were certainly aghast at the thought that such areas might be deprived of railway service, thus ending virtually all hope of industrial development.
It was heartwarming to find that while the economic position of the railroads is given consideration in the general findings of the MacPherson report the government in presenting Bill C-120 has made its legislation so comprehensive that questions such as the future industrial development of the areas concerned will be taken into account and considered very carefully before any permission to abandon lines is given. As I have just said, it is my hope that this question of the pos-

Railway Act
sible abandonment of railway lines in areas of slow industrial growth should be considered very carefully in conjunction with the policy of the government as expressed through the Department of Industry, and the area development agencies which are working to encourage industrial expansion where it has previously not taken place. It would surely be foolhardy to promote the abandonment of railway lines on one hand while seeking to achieve industrial expansion in those areas on the other because, once the railways are gone, any hope of industrial expansion would be extremely slight.

speechtext:
In the few moments left I have a few thoughts I should like to place before the house. I do so with hesitation because, coming from a seacoast constituency I am to a considerable degree a layman when I discuss railway line abandonment on the prairies. Nevertheless we in the city of Vancouver have an interest in this subject, inasmuch as we are exporters of a great deal of the grain which is grown in the prairie provinces, in the province of Alberta and on into Saskatchewan.
With the trend toward the shipment of larger quantities of grain across the Pacific we would like to ship more and more prairie grain from Vancouver. Indeed we are discussing at the present time the building of additional facilities so as to be able to handle more grain through that port, and provide the facilities needed for prairie producers to export their products to world markets as expeditiously as they can now be exported through the head of the lakes.
I wish to point out to hon. members opposite that when we pick up a railway map of Saskatchewan we see crosshatched on it more railway lines than one is likely to see on any other map anywhere in the world. I think it is safe to say that Saskatchewan is served by more railway lines operating uneconomically than any other spot on earth. In view of this fact, the question of rail line abandonment is academic. Of course railway lines must be altered in order that transportation may be placed upon a more economic basis. Our problem today is to get this done expeditiously enough that the United States to the south, which is rapidly overhauling its own transportation arrangements and improving its facilities for handling grain, does not reach a point where it becomes

highly competitive with us in moving grain to the Pacific coast and exporting across the Pacific to areas to which, because of an antipathy toward the Soviet world, there has been no great anxiety up to now to send commodities. However in the near future we can envisage the United States competing with our exports to these areas. It is only because of the political relationship between the United States and the communist world that we have been given some temporary advantage in selling our grain through the Pacific ports. So it would be unwise to place any moratorium upon the process of upgrading grain handling facilities in western Canada, thus losing the advantage we have, and damaging the prospect of keeping for Canadians an export market which is bound to continue for a considerable time.
As I say, I am not qualified to discuss this question in detail or at any length. Nevertheless I believe we should give consideration to the points I have raised and realize that upon the efficiency of our rail transport system may depend the future of a vital market, a highly competitive market which our neighbour to the south is prepared to enter.
